7.0.s.en: (1) The healing of the centurion's servant

7.0.0.en: After Christ finished His teaching on the plain, He entered the city of Capernaum, one of the largest towns of Galilee, north of the land of the Jews, in order to show the practical application of His commandments about love and compassion toward others.

7.1.0.en: The centurion: a rank in the Roman army, the one responsible for commanding a hundred soldiers. He had a servant who was struck by a severe illness that nearly cost him his life; Matthew mentions that he was palsied, that is, paralyzed. The centurion was distinguished by his love for his servants. Here St. Luke addresses the problem of slavery that prevailed at that time, in which domination and cruelty appeared. Here, however, he declares to us the ideal situation in the love of a master for his servants, as the love of the head of a household for his servants, or of a superior for those under him, ought to be: a love that shows itself in a special care no less than a father's love for his children.

7.1.1.en: The Gentile centurion asks Christ to heal his servant, and we shall see Christ's welcome of this, and even His praise of the Gentiles because they are His children. St. Luke took an interest in this story because he writes to the Gentiles.

7.2.0.en: The centurion felt unworthy to meet Christ because he was a Gentile, so he sent the elders of the Jews, that is, their leaders, to intercede for him before Christ so that his servant might be healed.

7.2.1.en: Here the importance of intercession appears, and it carries within it the humility of the one who seeks intercession, which gladdens the heart of God. The faith of this centurion in the power of Christ to heal also appears. The centurion's love for his servant is shown as well by his sending the elders of the Jews to Christ.

7.3.0.en: The elders of the Jews interceded before Christ, beseeching Him to come and heal the servant, although the centurion had not asked them for Christ to come, but only for the servant to be healed. They showed that this centurion was worthy to receive the blessing of his servant's healing from the hand of Christ, because his heart was full of love, not only for pagans like himself but for the Jews also; for he had built them a synagogue in Capernaum for the reading of the Holy Scriptures, spiritual sermons and prayers.

7.3.1.en: Love gives you grace in the eyes of all and opens closed doors for you, so help those around you as much as you can.

7.4.0.en: Christ went with the elders of the Jews toward the centurion's house. When He drew near and the centurion learned of it, he sent his friends to Christ to make clear his request. He did not mean for Christ to come to him, because he was not worthy of that, and because he knew that the Law of the Jews decrees that a Jew who enters the house of a Gentile is defiled until the evening. So he only begs that Christ command, and the servant will be healed.

7.4.1.en: Here the difference between the faith of the centurion and the faith of the elders becomes clear: he trusts that the word of Christ is sufficient for healing, whereas the elders believed that the touch of Christ's hand heals. The Gospel of Matthew mentions that the centurion met Christ (but it means that his friends met Christ), for they represent him and speak his words.

7.5.0.en: The centurion explains his faith that the word of Christ is sufficient for healing, because by virtue of his position he knows that his commands are sufficient to move the soldiers under him so that they carry out the work required of them. Therefore he believed that Christ is able, by His authority, to command the sickness and it will depart from his servant, and this is a clear faith in the divinity of Christ.

7.6.0.en: Christ glorified the faith of this centurion and esteemed it above the faith of the Jews themselves, to whom He was sent, and this glorification proclaims Christ's love and His concern for the salvation of the whole world. And He commanded the servant's healing, as is understood from the following verse.

7.7.0.en: The centurion's friends, together with the elders of the Jews, returned to the house after Christ had departed, and found the servant, who had been about to die, restored to health, and they rejoiced at the work of God.

7.8.s.en: (2) The raising of the son of the widow of Nain

7.8.0.en: After the healing of the centurion's servant, which signifies care for the salvation of the Gentiles and love for strangers, Christ moved from Capernaum toward the village of Nain, which is 25 miles from it, and with Him were a large number of His disciples and the crowds who loved to hear His teaching. God's purpose in taking this crowd along was to show them a great miracle to confirm their faith, namely, the raising of a dead man.

7.9.0.en: The Jews were accustomed to bury their dead outside the cities, so as not to catch diseases and not to be defiled by them. An only son of his mother, who was a widow, had died, and her grief was intense, because after losing her provider, who was her husband, her hope, who was her son, had died also. Hearts sympathized with her, and a large number from the city went out to comfort and support her. She is a symbol of the soul that has lost its Bridegroom, who is God, and then lost its life and itself, which is its only son. So Christ's concern for her is concern for the weak soul that has no support or hope.

7.10.0.en: Christ showed His tenderness to this woman with words that reassured her so that she would not weep, but He was not content with words, as human beings are; He accompanied them with a positive deed, raising the dead man.

7.10.1.en: Try to join your kind words with deeds by which you help others in their needs and troubles.

7.11.0.en: Because of Christ's majesty when He touched the bier, the bearers stood still, understanding that He wanted something. Then, by the authority of His divinity, He commanded the dead young man to rise. For He is the Resurrection and the Life, who is able to grant salvation and life to everyone over whom sin has gained mastery and who has lost the ability to live the spiritual life. And because the woman was very weak and the young man was dead and unable to ask anything of God, Christ took the initiative and performed the miracle without anyone asking Him.

7.11.1.en: Be confident that God loves you and meets your needs even if you do not ask Him, how much more if you ask Him and persist in asking.

7.12.0.en: The dead man rose and sat up, and showed that he had regained his life by speaking with the crowd, and perhaps he thanked Christ and glorified God. Everyone was amazed at what happened, including his mother, so Christ helped her by bringing the young man to her embrace. For He is God, who alone is able to restore life to every grieving and despairing soul like this woman.

7.13.0.en: From the power of the miracle, the crowds felt the fear of God, and remembered the prophets Elijah and Elisha, who raised the dead, so they glorified God, seeing in Christ a prophet like the prophets of old; yet Christ commanded the young man by the authority of His divinity and he rose at once, whereas the prophets asked God and so raised the dead.

7.14.0.en: Because of the greatness of the miracle, news of it spread throughout all the surrounding land of Judea.

7.15.s.en: (3) Christ's discourse about John the Baptist

7.15.0.en: John spoke with his disciples about Christ, His works and His teachings, to bind them to His love. Then he asked them whether He might be the Christ who was awaited, and they did not know the answer. So he said to them, Let us send two of you to ask Him plainly whether He is the Messiah. Two went to Christ and asked Him as John had commanded them. John was certain that He was the Christ, for the Holy Spirit had revealed it to him at His baptism, but he intended to declare this to his disciples so that they would follow Christ. This shows the humility of the Baptist and his emptying of himself.

7.15.1.en: Would you accept that another be honored and you not be honored? And do you seek to put others forward in honor in your place?

7.16.0.en: When the two disciples reached Christ, they saw Him healing many of the sick (infirmities = diseases or defects) and casting out demons, and they heard from the crowds the reports of His miracles, such as the raising of the son of the widow of Nain. When they asked Jesus, He did not first answer them with a yes, but offered clear proof that He is the Messiah through the miraculous works that He does, which the prophets had foretold that the Messiah would do: healing the sick, raising the dead, and preaching to the poor the salvation that the Messiah would bring.

7.17.0.en: Christ warned the two disciples and all who heard, lest they doubt Him because of His being in the flesh or His coming sufferings and death. For He is God, able to do all things, as His miracles prove, and if He humbly bears being in the flesh, and His sufferings and death, it is for the sake of the salvation of mankind.

7.18.0.en: After John's two disciples departed, having become sure from His many miracles that this was the awaited Messiah, Christ seized the opportunity and began to speak to the crowds about John the Baptist. He asked them about his person and his standing, and imagined with the crowds, as they went out to the wilderness, that they would find some reeds of the wild cane swaying with the winds. He asked whether John was merely an ordinary person living in the wilderness like one reed among the wild reeds, and so He denies of John this comparison, that of a reed shaken by the wind, for he is not a man wavering in his thoughts and principles, but strong and steadfast.

7.18.1.en: Then Christ asks about John again, when the crowds went out to the wilderness: was it, one wonders, to see a man living in luxury, occupied with the delights of life, which He indicates by soft raiment? .. And Christ strongly denies this, for those who live delicately dwell in the palaces of kings which are in the cities, not in the austerity of the wilderness, thereby showing the Baptist's asceticism. Then He asks a third time about John, the distinguished man who lives in the asceticism of the wilderness: is he a prophet because of his powerful teaching and his self-denial? .. And Christ answers, saying that he is greater than the ordinary prophets known among the Jews.

7.18.2.en: Do not be merely a person living in the world, eating and drinking and doing the material worldly works, moved by the currents of the world. Rather, you are the light of the world and the salt of the earth ... an image of Christ in all your words and works.

7.19.0.en: Christ refers to the prophecy of Malachi 3:1), (which spoke of John as an angel, that is, a messenger who prepares the way for the proclamation of Christ and His redemption.

7.20.0.en: Christ declares that the Baptist is not only a great prophet but the greatest of the men of the Old Testament. Then He adds a new truth, namely the loftiness of the grace of the New Testament above life under the Law in the Old Testament, since Christians in the Church receive the Holy Sacraments and the Holy Spirit also works in the means of grace to a greater degree than the sons of the Old Testament longed to see and behold these glories. So the least believer in the Church has God reigning over his heart and delighting him with His grace more greatly than what the sons of the Old Testament received, including John the Baptist.

7.20.1.en: There is another opinion, that the one meant by the least is Christ, who is younger than John by six months, and yet He is greater than John and than all mankind.

7.21.0.en: Then Christ speaks of the Baptist's popularity, and refers to it as all the people, that is, people generally, and even the greatest sinners such as the tax collectors, who declared their repentance, glorifying the righteous and holy God and their need for the baptism of repentance which they received from the hand of John.

7.22.0.en: Sadly, none departed from the consensus of the people except the leaders of Jewish religious thought, namely the Pharisees and the lawyers, who held to the Law literally. They became proud and boasted of their knowledge and their literal fulfillment of the Law, and so rejected repentance and the baptism of John, that is, the voice of God and His counsel which He had sent to them by the mouth of the Baptist.

7.23.0.en: The Pharisees rejected repentance and the baptism of John, and likewise the teachings of Christ, so Jesus gave them an illustrative parable to show them the hideousness of their rejection and the ignorance into which they fall. It is as though children were playing in the town market-place and divided themselves into two groups, one of which sang in the hope that the other would rejoice and dance, but it was not moved; then the same group tried to mourn so that the other group would weep, and again it was not moved, that is, it refused to respond to joy or to sorrow. What is meant here by the songs is the joyful spiritual teachings, that is, the good news of the New Testament that Christ brought, over which hearts should dance with joy in a spiritual dance and not a bodily one; as for the mourning, it is the Baptist's stern teachings which call people to repentance and to weeping over their sins.

7.24.0.en: The Jews rejected the teachings of John the Baptist and considered him wicked, having a devil, because of his severe asceticism, although he lived a life of austerity in order to proclaim the vanity of the world and the importance of repentance and of life with God.

7.25.0.en: On the contrary, Christ lived in the city, eating and drinking like the others around Him, and lived in righteousness an ordinary life like ordinary human beings, to make the possibility of the spiritual life easy for them, and He mingled with everyone, even sinners and tax collectors. So the Pharisees rejected His teachings also, because of His lack of asceticism, and they even insulted Him and described Him as a lover of food and drink, who loves to mingle with sinners because He is a sinner.

7.26.0.en: As for true Wisdom, that is, the hypostasis of the incarnate Word, He was glorified and justified only by those who repented through John's baptism and those who believed in Christ, for the children of Wisdom are the children of God who believe in Him. Do not hasten to condemn, but give heed to the voice of God which you hear and learn from others, however different their personalities may be.

7.27.s.en: (4) The sinful woman in the Pharisee's house

7.27.0.en: Because of the importance of this passage, the Church places it in her daily prayer, in the Second Watch of the Midnight Prayer in the Agpeya, for the deep spiritual meanings needed by everyone who keeps vigil and cares for his spiritual life. The Pharisees' hostility to Christ had not yet increased at the beginning of His ministry, so this Pharisee thought to become acquainted with His person, and therefore invited Him to a feast in his house; and Christ did not refuse, but seized it as an opportunity for service and preaching.

7.28.0.en: This woman was famous for her sin, which was probably adultery, and she came without invitation to the Pharisee's house to offer her love to Christ, of whom she had heard, and she may have seen and heard Him before, and she brought with her a flask of sweet perfume. She is, of course, not Mary the sister of Lazarus, who poured the ointment on Christ in Bethany near Jerusalem, because the place here is in Galilee and the woman here is a sinner, and those present objected to her approaching Christ because of her sin, whereas those present objected to Mary the sister of Lazarus because of the high value of the ointment and the poor's having a greater claim to it than Christ. And here it is in the house of Simon the Pharisee, whereas the other was in the house of Simon the leper (Mt 26:6-13; Mk 14:3-5; Jn 12:3-8).

7.29.0.en: At feasts the Jews were accustomed to have each person sit on a couch or sofa (a bench or a divan) while they ate at the table, so these couches were placed around the table and a person reclined, leaning on the elbow of his left arm on the table with his head resting on his left hand, and ate with his right hand, while his legs stretched out in front of him on the couch, and since he bent his knees, his feet were behind him and not in the direction of the table. So when this woman entered, she went toward Christ and stood before His feet, then knelt and began to weep in repentance for her many sins, feeling unworthy to draw near to Christ the Righteous, and with the abundance of her tears she wet His feet. Here she is a symbol of the repentant soul, which wants to know the way of the new life through the footsteps of Christ, and even wants Him to enter and walk within her heart, and when He is soiled with the filth of her sins, she offers the tears of her repentance so that God may accept her and remove from her all her evils.

7.29.1.en: These tears point to the water of Baptism, which washes away all of man's defilement, and to the tears of repentance in the sacrament of confession, which remove sin.

7.29.2.en: And the woman found nothing more precious than the crown of her head, that is, her hair, with which to wipe the feet of Christ, declaring her lowliness and humility before Him; her crown is the feet of Christ.

7.29.3.en: And the longings of her love stirred toward Christ, whose love, forgiveness and tenderness she trusts, so she began to kiss His feet. She also expressed her love by pouring the perfume on His feet and anointing them with it, since she did not feel worthy to pour it on His head, as was the custom of the Jews in welcoming their guests, but with humility she anointed His feet with it.

7.29.4.en: If you offer your repentance with humility, faith and love, you receive the forgiveness of your sins, and even Christ's honoring of you. Examine yourself every day about your sins, so that you may return in humble repentance, and the feelings of your love toward God may be stirred, and you may receive His mercies.

7.29.5.en: When the Pharisee saw this sinful woman touching Christ, who was probably an adulteress as we mentioned, because her sin was known in the city, and found no objection from Christ, although this is contrary to the Law and to the prevailing custom that the righteous keep away from the wicked, he said within himself that Christ was an ordinary person, because if He were a prophet He would know that she was a sinner and would refuse to let her touch Him, forgetting a more important matter, namely that the awaited Messiah would come to save sinners and not to keep them away from Him, and that sinners, if they repent and touch Him, are cleansed of their uncleanness.

7.29.6.en: Do not be hasty in judging others, and lift up your heart in a short prayer that God may guide you, so that you may see all sides of the matter and the truth may be revealed to you.

7.30.0.en: Christ knew what was in Simon's mind, and this proves His divinity, but He did not embarrass him by declaring what was in his mind; rather, with gentleness He asked his permission to say something to him, that is, to make clear to him his error, but through a practical parable that brings the spiritual idea near to his understanding.

7.30.1.en: If others wrong you, do not be angry, but with gentleness you can persuade them and win them.

7.31.0.en: The creditor is God, and the two debtors, one of whom owed ten times the other, and by the one with the great debt is meant the sinful woman because of her many sins known in the city, while the one with the small debt is Simon the Pharisee, because he held to the Law but fell into pride, condemnation and failure in the duties of hospitality.

7.32.0.en: When the owner of the money found that the debtors were unable to pay their debts, he forgave them both out of love, for all human beings are unable to pay their debts toward God because everyone has fallen into sin. Then Christ asked Simon: Which of the debtors, do you think, loves and feels the love of the owner of the money more than the other?

7.33.0.en: Simon gave an answer, namely that the one with the greater debt would feel the forgiveness and love of the owner of the money more than the other, and so would love him for his great kindness to him. And Christ commended his answer.

7.34.0.en: After the introductory parable, Christ made a comparison between the love of the Pharisee and the love of the sinful woman for Christ, to show her greatness and distinction. So He said to Simon that among the duties of hospitality is the washing of the guest's feet, because walking in open shoes, that is, sandals, on dusty ground must make the feet dirty, so the first thing the guest needs is to have his feet washed. But Simon did not do this, whereas the woman washed Christ's feet, not with water but with something greater, namely the tears of her repentance, and wiped them not with an ordinary towel but with the crown of her head, which is her hair. She made up for the Pharisee's lack and shortcoming in the duties of hospitality by her distinguished love.

7.35.0.en: Among the duties of hospitality is showing love by kissing the guest on his head or cheek, and in this too Simon fell short, and this woman made up for it with great humility by kissing the feet of Christ, not only one kiss but many kisses declaring her love and longings.

7.36.0.en: Among the duties of hospitality also is anointing the guest's head with oil, that is, fragrant perfume, which refreshes him, and this too Simon did not do, and this woman did it, pouring the perfume on the feet of Christ with humility. The most precious thing she had she offers at His feet, because she feels unworthy to place it on His head as is customary.

7.37.0.en: Because of this distinguished love of the sinful woman, God granted her great forgiveness that removes her many sins. But as for one whose love is little like Simon, who confined himself to giving a feast for Christ and whose pride hindered him from believing in Him, only a little of his sins will be forgiven.

7.37.1.en: God values your love even if it is little like Simon's, and He is ready to bless your life and your house by entering them. But if you have great love like the sinful woman, then whatever your sins, they will all be forgiven. For Simon was not justified from his sins, but merely received a blessing from Christ, whereas the woman received complete forgiveness and glorification from Christ.

7.38.0.en: Christ declared, by the authority of His divinity, the forgiveness of all this woman's sins, so that afterward she would be famous in the city and all the world not for her sins but for her great love by which she received complete forgiveness.

7.39.0.en: Those reclining at table, who were Pharisees and friends of Simon, objected with pride to Christ's forgiveness of the woman, despising His words, because the one who has authority to forgive is God alone, whereas Jesus in their eyes was merely an ordinary man and not even a prophet. Their pride prevented them from understanding the parable of the debtors and what Christ showed of this woman's love for Him.

7.39.1.en: Beware of pride, for it blinds the heart, so that a person is unable to understand God's words and His guidance sent through those around him.

7.40.0.en: Since the Pharisees did not understand, Christ blessed the woman, declaring the greatness of her faith, which the Pharisees were unable to attain, and which appeared in practice in the tears of her repentance and humility at His feet, and in her love in the perfume she poured out, so she received forgiveness and salvation, and deserved to have her heart filled with peace with which to go on and complete her life. It is practical faith, joined to repentance, humility and love, that saves you, and not merely theoretical faith, which the demons share with you.

7.40.1.en: The parable of the sower. The rebuking of the winds. The demoniac of the country of the Gadarenes. The woman with the issue of blood
